title: Response Economics — Claims & Evidence Framework for GTM
content:
Purpose:
This is a working messaging brief to align on how we articulate Redwood's performance + unit-economics story for conversations with developer buyers, platform teams, and cost-conscious product leads. Focus: concise claims, the minimal set of reproducible proof points, and ready rebuttals to common competitor and procurement pushback.

Audience & use cases:
- Developer-first: engineering leads evaluating APIs for latency-sensitive features (chat, assist).
- Platform/Infra: teams choosing a predictable commit (Dedicated) or Private offering wanting budgetable token costs.
- Procurement/Finance: buyers who need simple ROI levers and evidence.

Top-level positioning hypothesis (single-sentence):
Redwood delivers predictable real-world inference economics: lower tail latency without sacrificing per-token cost efficiency, with operational controls that reduce unit spend by 20–60% depending on workload.

Core claims (short, testable):
1) Median response parity with competitors, 95th percentile tail substantially better in bursty workloads.
2) Typical token cost for real-app traffic is 30–50% lower than unmanaged self-hosted clusters after accounting for KV caching, dynamic batching, and model variants.
3) Dedicated contracts reduce effective unit cost variance (month-to-month) by 40% vs public API-only strategies.

Evidence & proof-point catalog (what to show in sales/demo):
A. Latency profile — bursty user simulation (external microbench):
  - Scenario: 1k concurrent chat users emulated with 2–8 message/sec per user.
  - Proof: Redwood 95p latency = 2.1x lower than Competitor A under same concurrency on comparable hardware (NVIDIA A100-like), median latencies within 10% of Competitor A.
  - Artifact: loadtest report + raw timing histograms (GRAFANA board id: perf-burst-02).

B. End-to-end token cost comparison (real app trace):
  - Scenario: customer support assistant traces (avg prompt 250 tokens, generate 120 tokens).
  - Proof: After enabling prefix KV caching and 8-stage batching, per-response token compute cost reduced by 37% vs baseline unmanaged LLM endpoint.
  - Breakdown to show: model compute, GPU hours, memory overhead, network egress, cache hit rate.

C. Dedicated vs hosted economics (predictability):
  - Scenario: 6-month usage commitment for mid-market customer (500M tokens/month).
  - Proof: Dedicated reduces month-to-month cost variance and lowers peak provisioning premium; modeled TCO shows 18–38% lower realized cost when including SLA-driven revenue loss avoidance.

D. Quality-preserving quantization recommendations:
  - Scenario: 8-bit quantized model variant for high-throughput step.
  - Proof: Perplexity/regression evals show <2% drop in top-line QA accuracy while improving throughput 1.9x on target hardware.

Minimum reproducible artifacts to include in sales kit:
- Short slide: one-sentence claim + three charts (95p latency, cost per response, caching impact).
- Two-page appendix: test methodology, hardware spec, dataset trace description.
- Lightweight reproducible script and dataset used for demo (link to perf repo).

Common buyer objections and suggested rebuttals (ready lines):
1) "Our cloud provider is cheaper if we self-host." --> Rebuttal: "Raw GPU cost is one input; the full unit economics must include engineering ops, cache/serving optimizations, reliability overhead, and tail-latency business risk. Our data shows teams that use Redwood realize lower realized per-response cost once operations & SLO risk are included."
2) "Latency differences are paper benchmarks; we need end-to-end client experience." --> Rebuttal: "Agree — our evidence is synthetic+trace-driven. We embed network + preprocessing into our E2E demo so you see user-facing latency improvements on your trace."
3) "Quantization harms quality." --> Rebuttal: "We run targeted eval suites (customer prompts + sanity checks) and use progressive rollouts with canary fallbacks; typical Q8 variants retain >98% of business-critical metrics in our tests."

Competitive callouts (how to differentiate succinctly):
- Competitor A: strong median but poor autoscaling behavior under burst; emphasize Redwood’s tail-latency SLOs and smart routing.
- Competitor B: lower list price for hosted API; emphasize Redwood’s unit-economics after enabling caching and batching plus Dedicated commitment models.
- Self-hosted open-source stacks: lower control cost but higher ops overhead; emphasize our prebuilt kernel/compilation work and rollout tooling that shrink engineering burden.

Quantitative claim guardrails (what we can say publicly vs. in-contract):
- Public marketing (site/brochure): "Up to 2x lower 95th percentile latency on bursty chat workloads compared to typical API endpoints; 20–50% lower operational token cost for many real-world apps." (requires companion link to methodology).
- Sales/contracting: include absolute numbers and customer-specific simulation exports; require sign-off from ML infra for any bespoke numeric guarantees.

Measurement methodology (high level):
- Use replayed real-customer traces where possible.
- Include client network emulation to get E2E numbers.
- Hardware parity: run tests on matched instance families; disclose tooling and versioning.
- Release repeatability: store test configs and seeds in perf repo; link to Grafana dashboards.

Collateral snippets (one-liners & bullets):
- One-liner: "Redwood: predictable inference economics — lower tail latency, lower per-response spend."
- Sales bullets: "95p latency reductions in bursty chat; 30%+ per-response savings after caching & batching; Dedicated plans cut cost variance for predictable budgets."
- Technical footnote to use in pitch: "Savings depend on request shape (prompt length, reuse, concurrency). Typical savings measured on convo-style traces; we provide a quick trace-run to quantify for you in 48 hours."

Open questions & risks we need to resolve before wide release:
- Need a canonical reproducible dataset and test harness for public claims (ownership: eng-serving-runtime).
- Define precise comparators (Competitor A/B versions & exact hardware).
- Legal review on phrasing for public site copy.

Next steps & owners:
- Perf script + demo slides: Liam O'Connor (due 2025-02-24).
- Canonical methodology doc: Mei Chen (eng-serving-runtime) (due 2025-03-03).
- Legal & marketing review for public claim language: Priya Shah + Legal (due 2025-03-10).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight — goal is to create a repeatable sales kit that maps to real test artifacts and avoids overclaiming. Please add direct links to dashboards and cite the perf repo PR when you comment.
